title: IWC MK XI 6B/346 ROYAL AIR FORCE ISSUED
description: The IWC Mark XI 6B/346 holds a special place among collectors of vintage military watches. Issued to the British military from the late 1940s, these 36mm pilot’s watches are not only virtually indestructible, but also superbly balanced and legible on the wrist. Most Mark XIs you’ll come across have a circled T on the dial, indicating tritium lume, but they were originally issued with radium dials. It wasn’t until the 1960s that these were replaced with less radioactive tritium dials. This example dates from the very beginning of Mark XI production in 1948 and is easily one of the best we have ever seen. The stainless steel fixed-lug case is untouched, and a soft-iron inner cage protects the hand-wound calibre 89 from magnetic fields. The dial has survived in amazing condition, with pumpkin-toned lume and no imperfections. After a full service, the watch is running beautifully at +2 s/d, with 280° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error, nearly 80 years after it was made. The Mark XI went on to inspire many later IWC pilot’s watches, and this is as fine an example as you’ll find.

title: LEMANIA CHRONOGRAPH MONOPUSHER 'MOA ISSUED'
description: From the mid-1940s until around 1970, Lemania was the exclusive supplier of mechanical chronographs to the British military. To meet the Ministry of Defence’s specifications, these were all monopusher chronographs, with the start, stop and reset functions controlled by a single button at 2 o’clock, which helped prevent the chronograph from being started accidentally. In 1969, the MoD published a new specification, DEF-STAN 66-4, which was amended the following year to allow two-pusher chronographs. From then on, military chronograph supply was dominated by four manufacturers, all using the Valjoux 7733 movement: Hamilton, CWC, Newmark and Precista. The Lemania 6BB/924-3306 here was issued to the Royal Air Force in 1965 and is easily one of the nicest examples out there. The tritium lume on the markers has aged to an intense pumpkin hue, and the case is largely free of marks. Following a recent service, the watch is running beautifully at +5 s/d, with 250° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX OYSTER PERPETUAL 36 PINK EXPLORER DIAL 116034 FULL SET
description: As a lover of vintage watches, I must admit that one of my guilty pleasures in the modern Rolex range is the 36mm Oyster Perpetual. It is simple and slim, yet it comes in fun, playful designs of a kind Rolex has rarely offered over the years. The introduction of colourful dials in recent years really propelled the popularity of the OP line, but Rolex began experimenting quite a bit earlier. The Ref. 116034 here dates from 2017 and has a fluted bezel and a very cool “Explorer” dial, with Arabic numerals at 3, 6 and 9. Instead of the usual white, however, all the hour markers are pink. And no, this isn’t a custom dial: Rolex really did make it this way. Nearly a decade later, these have become something of a fan favourite. They are hard to find in this part of the world, having been more popular in Asia, and are incredibly fun to wear. This example recently came through Rolex’s Certified Pre-Owned (CPO) programme and is supplied with its original box, warranty card and Rolex CPO card. The movement is running perfectly at +1 s/d, with 280° amplitude and a 0.0 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX SEA DWELLER 16600 TRITIUM DIAL FULL SET
description: The Sea-Dweller was perhaps the only Rolex sports model created truly out of necessity: the state-of-the-art dive watch Rolex offered at the time, the Submariner, simply wasn’t up to the demands of a rapidly evolving subsea industry. The Ref. 1665 was introduced in 1967 and sold to civilians from around 1971. In 1978, the Ref. 16660 “Triple Six” was released and produced alongside the 1665. It offered an improved water resistance of 1,220 metres, thanks to a more robust case, an enlarged helium escape valve and, for the first time on a Rolex dive watch, a sapphire crystal. The Ref. 16600 here is the third iteration of the Sea-Dweller. Released in 1988, it remained in production for a whopping two decades before being retired in 2008. The case design was largely unchanged from the Triple Six, and for good reason: it wears beautifully on the wrist, and very differently from modern Sea-Dwellers. This example dates from 1997 and has a lovely tritium dial that has taken on a beautiful creamy patina, which is rather rare on a 16600. The watch was originally sold in Japan, and the case has been kept in amazing condition, having been only very lightly polished. The original 93160 bracelet has no stretch. The movement has just been serviced and is running beautifully at 0 s/d, with 295° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. The watch comes with all its original boxes, accessories and paperwork. A beautiful neo-vintage Sea-Dweller.

title: ROLEX DAY-DATE 18039 18K WHITE GOLD
description: It’s no secret that I love vintage and neo-vintage Day-Dates. They are slim and classy, and they represent mind-boggling value compared with both vintage sports models and modern Day-Dates. The 180xx series was introduced in the late 1970s and represents the second generation of the Day-Date line-up. It was fitted with the updated calibre 3055 movement and was the first Day-Date to feature a quick-set date. This small but significant upgrade makes the watch much easier to set when it is worn only occasionally as part of a collection. The Ref. 18039 here dates from 1983 and has an 18k white gold case, which was produced in much smaller numbers than the yellow gold version. The watch has been enjoyed over the years but has amazingly survived in fantastic condition, with an unpolished case. The dial, hands, German-language day wheel and date wheel were replaced by Rolex during a service last year. The movement runs beautifully at +3 s/d, with 291° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. The original guarantee papers and booklets are still present, as is the NFC Rolex service card.

title: CHOPARD L.U.C. QUATTRO 16/1903 FULL SET
description: In 2000, Chopard surprised the watch world with one of haute horlogerie’s most interesting movements in some time: the L.U.C Cal. 1.98, with four barrels and an impressive nine-day power reserve. Amazingly, the team led by Chopard co-president Karl-Friedrich Scheufele fitted all of this into a compact 38mm case (Ref. 16/1863) just 9.5mm thick. The 16/1863 received COSC certification as well as the Geneva Seal. In 2007, the brand updated the “Quattro” line with the 16/1903 series (Mk II), and again in 2011 with the 16/1926 series (Mk III), which had larger cases. This example is from the second generation and has a 38mm 18k white gold case. Compared with the first-generation 16/1863, the 16/1903 has a bolder dial design. A white guilloché centre is surrounded by a contrasting black ring carrying the Arabic hour numerals, with a date and small seconds subdial at 6 o’clock and the power reserve indicator at 12 o’clock. The watch has been preserved in amazing condition over the years, with barely any wear. It comes with all its original boxes, paperwork and accessories. Neo-vintage dress pieces are finally getting the attention they deserve. With the current-generation Quattro starting at over £37,000, this remains one of the most overlooked watches from a top Swiss manufacture.

title: ROLEX SEA-DWELLER 1665 GREAT WHITE MK1
description: The Sea-Dweller was perhaps the only Rolex sports model created truly out of necessity: the state-of-the-art dive watch Rolex offered at the time, the Submariner, simply wasn’t up to the demands of a rapidly evolving subsea industry. The Ref. 1665 was produced from 1967 to 1983, although it was only sold to civilians from around 1971. In the first years of production, the depth rating and “Sea-Dweller” text were printed in red, and these watches are affectionately known as “Double Red Sea-Dwellers”. From 1977 to 1983, five further dial variations appeared (Mk0 to Mk4), with the Sea-Dweller name and depth rating now printed in white, earning the nickname “Great White”. The present example has a Mk1 dial, which is seen from around the 5.1m to early 6m serial ranges. Although these ranges overlap with Mk2 and Mk3 examples, Mk1s are, based on our own observations, much rarer. Having spent its entire life on the Scottish coast, this watch remains in fantastic condition. The case has been polished, but probably no more than once or twice. The dial is perfect, with the lume on the markers and hands aged to an even, creamy hue. The original silver date wheel is present, and the insert has faded beautifully to a grey-lavender tone. The original 93150/580 bracelet with F-coded (1981) clasp retains all its links and shows minimal stretch. The movement was serviced this year and is running like a dream at 0 s/d, with 280° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX SEA-DWELLER 16660 'TRIPLE SIX' MATTE DIAL
description: In the Rolex dive watch lineage of the past 70 years, the Sea-Dweller 16660 “Triple Six”, introduced in 1978, arguably represented the single biggest technological leap forward. Produced alongside its predecessor, the 1665, it offered a significantly improved water resistance of 1,220 metres. This came from a more robust case, an enlarged helium escape valve and, for the first time on a Rolex dive watch, a sapphire crystal. It set a new benchmark for professional dive watches, and nearly 50 years later, one could argue that these features are still the blueprint for the modern dive watch. In the early years of production, Rolex fitted the 16660 with matte “Pallettoni” dials. In 1983/84, glossy “Bicchierini” dials were introduced, and they remained in use until the end of production. Despite having the lowest production numbers of any Sea-Dweller reference, the 16660 exists in a remarkable variety of dial executions, even more so than other transitional Rolex models of the period. These dials were made by several manufacturers, including Beyeler, Stern and Lemrich. This 1983 example has a Pallettoni dial made by Beyeler. The tritium lume on the markers and hands has aged to a rich, dark cream patina that contrasts wonderfully with the matte black dial, which itself has taken on a subtle tropical hue. As you can see, the watch has been used exactly as intended. The bezel has faded attractively, and the tritium pearl has developed a lovely warm tan. The case has been polished in the past but remains full and even, with no pinholes. It is fitted to its original 93160/592 bracelet with a P11 (November 1991) clasp, which is likely a service replacement. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at +4 s/d, with 290° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. We also replaced all the gaskets, and the watch passed a 10-bar pressure test. Examples like this make me fall in love with vintage Rolex over and over again.

title: HEUER CALCULATOR 150.633
description: In 1969, Heuer, alongside Breitling, Hamilton-Büren and Dubois Dépraz, unveiled the Calibre 11, one of the world’s first automatic chronograph movements. Heuer was quick to build a whole family of utilitarian sports chronographs around it, from the Monaco and the Carrera to the cushion-cased Autavia. There were a few oddballs among them too, and the Calculator has become one of the fan favourites. Introduced in 1972, the Calculator was originally designed for engineers, pilots and anyone else who regularly needed to multiply, divide or convert figures. Its rotating outer bezel works against a fixed inner scale to form a circular slide rule, so calculations can be read directly from the watch. It’s not a small watch, but its reasonable lug-to-lug length makes it surprisingly wearable. The Calculator was offered in two main versions. The models with symmetrical subdials, such as the Ref. 110.633, used the Calibre 12, with a 30-minute and a 12-hour register. The Ref. 150.633 here was powered by the Calibre 15, a simplified version of the Chronomatic movement with a running seconds subdial at 10 o’clock and a 30-minute counter at 2. The present example has a beautiful blue dial, which has been kept in fantastic condition over the years. The orange accents have kept their original colour, and the tritium lume has aged to an even, creamy hue. Following a recent health check, the movement is running beautifully at +6 s/d, with 271° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error.

title: HEUER AUTAVIA 1163 JO SIFFERT MEISTER DOUBLE SIGNED
description: Heuer introduced the Autavia in 1962 with the Ref. 2446, and over the following two decades released more than 90 variants of what would become its flagship sports chronograph. Early Autavias had round screw-back cases and three-register dials, with compressor cases following shortly afterwards. A major shift came in 1969, when Heuer, alongside Breitling, Hamilton-Büren and Dubois Dépraz, developed the Calibre 11, one of the world’s first automatic chronograph movements. The automatic Autavias moved to a cushion-shaped case, which remained in use until the quartz crisis brought Heuer’s golden era to an end. Among them, the 1163 T “Jo Siffert” is easily one of the most desirable, with its white dial and beautiful blue accents. Jo Siffert famously wore one almost constantly until his fatal accident in 1971. This example has survived in amazing condition. The white dial has taken on a gentle creamy patina, complemented by the tritium lume on the markers and hands, which has aged to the same gorgeous creamy hue. The blue accents on the markers and chronograph seconds hand have retained their full colour, as have the black inserts on the polished markers and the hour and minute hands. The icing on the cake is that the watch was originally retailed by Meister, the Zurich retailer that is still in business today, and the dial proudly bears the Meister signature. Double-signed Meister Heuers are few and far between, and to my knowledge, this is the only one currently for sale. The movement is running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 281° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. An amazing Heuer.

title: DOXA SUB 300T SYNCHRON
description: Originally founded in 1889 by Georges Ducommun in Le Locle, Doxa began as a traditional Swiss watchmaker. However, it was in the mid-twentieth century that the brand truly made its mark in the world of dive watches. Among dive watch enthusiasts, Doxa is widely recognised as a true innovator in purpose-built underwater tools. The tonneau-shaped SUB 300 and SUB 300T not only featured bold, forward-thinking designs but also introduced technical innovations such as the helium escape valve and the unidirectional bezel, features later adopted by industry giants such as Rolex and Omega. Like many other brands, Doxa was hit hard by the Quartz Crisis. The SUB 300T, introduced in 1968, was discontinued just a few years later in the mid-1970s, leaving relatively few original examples in circulation today. Thankfully, the brand has enjoyed a revival in recent years, with a series of well-received reissues that have reignited interest in these historically significant watches. The present example features the most recognisable iteration of the original SUB 300T, with its bright orange dial: a colour chosen following extensive underwater visibility testing. The case proudly carries the character it has earned over the years, while the tritium dial remains spotless. We have paired the watch with a period lobster-style bracelet, although it looks equally at home on a beads-of-rice bracelet or a NATO. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running at +4 s/d, with 290° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error. The watch has also passed a 5-bar pressure test. There are few vintage dive watches that combine historical importance, technical innovation, rarity, and outright awesomeness quite like the SUB 300T. Such a formidable watch.

title: UNIVERSAL GENÈVE POLEROUTER 'MICROTOR' 20368-1
description: For many vintage watch nerds such as myself, Universal Genève Polerouters hold a special place in our hearts. The elegant design, robust movements, and sheer variety of references within the line-up make the Polerouter one of the most rewarding watches to collect. It also helps that, for many years, these watches were readily available on the market and remarkably affordable (sadly, those glorious days are now behind us...). In the early 1950s, commercial aviation was rewriting the map. Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) pioneered a bold new route, charting a course over the magnetic North Pole to connect Los Angeles and Copenhagen faster than ever before. To mark the occasion, SAS turned to Universal Genève to create a watch worthy of this milestone in modern exploration. The result was a design by a young Gérald Genta, who would later go on to create some of the most iconic watches in horological history. At just 24 years old, he conceived the Polarouter (as it was initially named), issued to SAS pilots and crew, and built to perform in extreme conditions with both precision and style. It wasn’t long before its reputation extended far beyond the cockpit. The watch was soon renamed Polerouter, and the rest is history. Early Polerouters featured "bumper" automatic movements (such as the calibre 138SS), which we absolutely love—partly because of the satisfying bump you feel as the rotor reaches the end of its travel. In the mid-1950s, however, Universal Genève filed patent no. 329805, describing a revolutionary micro-rotor movement in which the winding rotor was integrated into the movement rather than mounted above it. This allowed the manufacture to produce some of the thinnest automatic movements of the era, including the calibre 218-9 found in this lovely ref. 20368-1. All the technicalities aside, a crosshair-dial, time-only Polerouter is simply gorgeous. This example has survived in wonderful condition over the years. The black dial with its silver rehaut is striking; the original dauphine hands, applied UG logo, and all of the original lume remain intact. The case is especially full on this one, and the engravings on the caseback are still beautifully crisp. We've paired the watch with these period stainless steel bracelet. The movement came to us running beautifully at +5 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.7 ms beat error. Putting a Polerouter on has never failed to put a smile on my face, and I hope this one brings as much joy to its next owner as it

title: FRANCK MULLER PERPETUAL CALENDAR 5850 QP FULL SET
description: If you were into watches in the 1990s and early 2000s, you’ll know that Franck Muller was one of the “hottest” brands on the market. It was particularly popular in Asia and often seen as a status symbol, thanks to its signature tonneau case and bold dial designs. Unfortunately, the brand’s popularity dropped significantly over the following two decades, perhaps because of the sheer number of models it introduced and heavy discounting, both in store and, in particular, on the secondary market. For us watch nerds, however, Franck Muller remains a formidable and highly respected brand, especially in its early years. Founded in 1991 by Franck Muller and Vartan Sirmakes, the brand quickly gained a reputation for serious watchmaking. Muller himself was widely regarded as one of the finest watchmakers of his generation, having spent years restoring and studying some of the most complicated watches ever made. In the early days, the brand focused heavily on high complications, producing perpetual calendars, tourbillons and minute repeaters. Its first watches were traditional complications that, from a distance, many would mistake for Patek Philippe or Breguet. They were produced in extremely small numbers and remain among the most collectible examples of early independent watchmaking. Soon afterwards, Franck Muller developed the style it is now best known for: the tonneau-shaped Cintrée Curvex. The perpetual calendar Ref. 5850 QP here dates from 1999 and perfectly illustrates what Franck Muller is all about. Its 32 × 38.5mm 18k yellow gold case houses the Franck Muller calibre 2800, which is based on the ETA 2892 but fitted with FM’s in-house perpetual calendar module. The date, moon phase, month and day/leap year subdials at 3, 6, 9 and 12 o’clock respectively are complemented by the bold exploding numerals. The watch has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at −3 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.6 ms beat error. Putting it on the wrist takes you straight back to Hong Kong at the turn of the millennium. What a time that was.

title: ENICAR SHERPA JET GRAPH 300 'MKIV'
description: In the 1960s and ’70s, numerous iconic chronographs emerged from historic manufacturers such as Rolex, Omega, Breitling, Universal Genève and Heuer. In the shadow of these big names, Enicar also produced a series of exceptional sports chronographs in the 1960s, which have gained a cult following among collectors. Enicar began as the Manufacture d’Horlogerie Ariste Racine in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, in 1913, founded by husband-and-wife duo Ariste Racine and Emma Blatt. A year later, the pair renamed the company “Enicar”: Racine spelt backwards. Over the following decades, Enicar steadily grew in popularity thanks to its exceptional quality for the price. At the 44th Basel Watch Fair in 1960, Enicar released the “Sherpa Graph”, which proved to be one of the brand’s most successful models, partly thanks to its association with legendary F1 driver Jim Clark, who famously wore one. Between 1960 and 1970, Enicar introduced a series of sports chronographs known as the “Graphs”: the Sherpa Graph, Aqua Graph, Jet Graph and Super Graph. The present example is the fourth and final iteration of the Jet Graph. Designed for pilots and frequent travellers, the Jet Graph adds a GMT function to the chronograph. It is powered by the Valjoux 724, a modified version of the famed Valjoux 72 with an added 24-hour hand. The Mk IV was made for only about a year, in 1969. Enicar did things its own way: the “reverse panda” three-register dial is complemented by playful details, including the vibrant red-orange chronograph hand, the chequered GMT hand, the 24-hour bezel and the red bezel pointer ring. The dial and hands are in great condition, with all the lume intact. The compressor case, supplied by Ervin Piquerez SA (EPSA) and similar to that of the Heuer Autavia, is in equally excellent condition and appears unpolished. Fewer than 500 Enicar “Graphs” are believed to have survived, making them among the rarest sports chronographs of the 1960s. This watch has recently been serviced and is running perfectly at −5 s/d, with 320° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error. An outstanding watch.

title: ROLEX GMT-MASTER 1675 TYPE C WIDE SWISS GILT DIAL
description: The GMT-Master 1675 is easily one of the most exciting references in vintage Rolex collecting. Not only did it go through numerous variations during more than 20 years of production, but thanks to its colourful bezels and the different lacquers, paints and lume used, each example has developed a truly individual character over the decades, often beautiful in very different ways. This 1966 example has a Type C gilt dial and is simply wonderful. The galvanic dial is gorgeous, with all the lume aged to a uniform, creamy hue. The case has been lightly polished in the past, and the 7836/382 bracelet has only mild stretch. The original “Pepsi” bezel has faded heavily in the blue section but retained its full red hue in the red half. The watch turns 60 this month and comes with its original boxes, wallet, guarantee and chronometer papers. It was serviced last year and is running smoothly at +2 s/d, with 250° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. There’s just nothing quite like a gilt 1675.

title: OMEGA JUMBO CHRONOGRAPH CAL. 33.3
description: In the world of Omega chronographs, the calibre 321 is by far the most famous movement, and deservedly so. It powered the CK2915, the very first Speedmaster, and since its recent revival it has once again become the flagship movement of the current Speedmaster range. However, its lesser-known ancestor, the cal. 33.3, is arguably more collectible and most certainly rarer. Based on a Lemania design and shared with Tissot within the SSIH group, the calibre 33.3 was introduced in the early 1930s and remained in production for around two decades. Despite that long run, fewer than 14,000 are believed to have been made. These movements powered a range of Omega chronographs, from snap-back models such as this one to water-resistant references such as the CK2077, original examples of which now fetch astronomical sums. The 33.3 is widely recognised as the predecessor of the cal. 321. Historical importance aside, it is also one of the most beautiful chronograph movements ever made. When this watch came through the door, I couldn’t wait to pop open the caseback and admire the incredibly well-kept cal. 33.3. The watch itself has also survived in outstanding condition, and its 37.5mm case is extremely large for the period. The white multi-scale dial has an outer tachymeter, a telemeter scale for calculating distance using the speed of sound, and an inner decimal ring. It is finished with gorgeous leaf hands and a chronograph seconds hand with a beautiful spade-shaped tail. The dial has a gentle creamy patina, and the printing has been lightly retouched in the past, as is the case with many examples from this period. More than 80 years on, the watch still runs remarkably well at +8 s/d, with 255° amplitude and a 1.2 ms beat error. It was made in Switzerland while the world was in the depths of the Second World War. Simply incredible.

title: AUDEMARS PIGUET CAL.2612 GREY DIAL
description: The Royal Oak is undoubtedly one of the most iconic watches of all time. It arguably saved Audemars Piguet, and Gérald Genta’s legendary 1972 design has shaped the brand ever since. Yet the manufacture produced an incredible range of watches both before and after the Royal Oak’s debut. Fast-forward to today, and the Royal Oak continues to dominate the brand’s image and demand. As a result, some fantastic 20th-century APs with exceptional craftsmanship fly under the radar and still offer remarkable value. The present example dates from the 1980s and is a wonderful product of its time. The 1970s and 80s were an incredibly difficult period for the Swiss watchmaking industry. Quartz made the mechanical movement all but obsolete in practical terms, almost overnight. Even the biggest brands scrambled to “adapt” to the new technology, and some didn’t survive long enough to try. Thankfully, AP just about made it through, and a few decades later, quartz APs from this era are fascinating to study and collect. This example has a 31mm 18k white gold stepped case with a beautiful grey dial. Mercifully, the two-hand design means we don’t have to witness a second hand ticking on a quartz watch. The watch was rarely worn and is unpolished, and the hallmarks on the caseback are as sharp as on day one. The original leather strap and 18k buckle are both present. A new battery has been fitted. A gorgeous AP that looks amazing on any wrist.

title: ROLEX DATEJUST 36 16014 TAPESTRY DIAL
description: It’s hard to beat a neo-vintage Datejust, especially one with a cool dial. The Rolex Datejust 160xx series was arguably the last generation with a truly vintage look: an acrylic crystal, drilled lugs, a slim case and, of course, a tritium dial. The Ref. 16014 here has a white gold bezel and a beautiful silver tapestry dial. These are easily among the most attractive Datejusts. The textured surface plays wonderfully with the light, and as an added Easter egg, the dials often age to cream or sometimes salmon. This one has an off-white hue. The watch came to us in amazing condition, with a minimally polished case and a spotless dial, with all the creamy tritium lume intact. The original 62510H bracelet with I-stamped clasp shows virtually no stretch. We have just serviced the watch, and it is running nicely at +3 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX DAY-DATE 18038 'BLUE DIAL' COLLECTOR SET
description: Despite the overwhelming popularity of sports watches, the Day-Date has always been Rolex’s flagship and top-of-the-range model. Introduced in the 1950s, its iconic design has barely changed in the seven decades since. The 180xx series represents the second main generation of the Day-Date line-up. It brought the updated calibre 3055 movement and was the first Day-Date with a quick-set date. (If you’ve ever owned a four-digit Day-Date, you’ll appreciate how much of a difference this makes…) This 1985 example is easily one of the most beautiful 18038s you’ll ever see. Its sunburst blue dial plays wonderfully with the light and offers a striking contrast to the 18k yellow gold case. The original bracelet shows minimal stretch after more than four decades, and the previously polished case remains strong. All the lume plots are intact, and the day and date wheels have taken on a lovely matching patina. There is minor oxidation on the hour markers. The watch comes with its original inner and outer boxes, leather notebook, wallet, calendar, tags, handkerchief, original guarantee papers and all the service papers. The movement is running beautifully at +2 s/d, with 281° amplitude and a 0 beat error. An absolutely stunning Day-Date that we are proud to present.

title: ROLEX EXPLORER II 16550 WGS CREAM DIAL
description: As far as “transitional” Rolex references go, the Explorer II 16550 is among the most interesting and desirable. Following the lukewarm commercial reception of the Ref. 1655 “Steve McQueen” (hard to imagine today), the 16550 was introduced with a new movement offering a quick-set date, hacking seconds and the novel addition of an independently adjustable GMT hand. Despite its short four-year production run, the 16550 went through several dial variations. Early examples had white gold surrounds (WGS) on the hour markers, while later ones switched to black surrounds. By far the most desirable are the so-called “cream dial” versions. Owing to a manufacturing imperfection, the dials of certain 16550s aged to a striking creamy tone, most commonly on WGS examples. This example dates from the very beginning of 16550 production, in 1984, and time has blessed it with a lovely creamy dial. The gentle off-white hue is complemented by the cream-toned tritium markers in their white gold surrounds and the tritium hands. The watch has been kept in amazing condition over the years. The case has been polished, but only lightly, and the original wide-font bezel is in equally good shape. The 78360/501B bracelet is a 2006 service replacement. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 271° amplitude and a 0.0 ms beat error. Cream-dial 16550s have become some of the most collectible vintage Rolex watches in recent years, and this is a fantastic example to enjoy every day.

title: AUDEMARS PIGUET 15048BA 18K YELLOW GOLD
description: We’ve waited years, but smaller dress watches are finally making a comeback. Since the introduction of the Royal Oak in 1972, Audemars Piguet’s identity has been inextricably linked with it. Half a century later, the Royal Oak’s popularity has only continued to rise, while many of AP’s dressier offerings from the 1990s and early 2000s have fallen into relative obscurity. Whether this is simply a result of the sports watch boom of the past decade is open to debate, but the unexpected outcome is that some truly wonderful watches from this era can still be bought at remarkably reasonable prices. The Ref. 15048 here has a 32 mm 18k yellow gold case and a matching gold dial. Thanks to its thin bezel, however, it wears more like a 34 mm and looks wonderful on the wrist. This example has clearly been admired rather than worn over the years. There’s barely any wear visible, even on the original leather strap and 18k yellow gold buckle. The watch has been freshly serviced and is running perfectly at +2 s/d, with 251° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. It comes with its original warranty papers and booklets. A prime example of how a beautiful precious-metal watch from a Holy Trinity brand needn’t cost tens of thousands of pounds.
